attempts.raw_response: She just laughed and said he'd better watch himself or his wife would hear of it, and he went away looking quite pleased with himself. Then I saw Mr. Westaway come to fetch her for the photographs, and really Mamma, I cannot tell you how strange it looked to see them together, after everything. He was so formal and proper, as if nothing had happened at all, and she walked off with him quite calmly, though I did notice she didn't let him take her arm. The whole thing put me quite out of sorts, I assure you, and I found myself wandering toward the garden where it was quieter. There were some other people I didn't know sitting on benches, and one young man nodded at me in a way that made me feel rather fluttered, but of course I didn't stop to talk. I do hope the breakfast doesn't start too late—I'm simply starving after all this excitement.

She just laughed in that way she has, you know the one, and said "Alfred, you old scandal, I like it very well indeed, and you may fetch me another cup of tea." And then she caught sight of me watching and gave me such a knowing look, as if we were in it together somehow. I did so want to stay and hear more, but Mamma was beckoning me across to where Lady Pemberton was holding forth about the flowers, and you know I cannot be rude about flowers to a lady who arranges them so beautifully. Wasn't it odd though? I had no idea Mrs. Westaway knew anyone so common. I thought she only moved in such elevated circles. Perhaps she is more versatile than we supposed. I do hope you are not too bored by all this gossip.

I was trying to place where I had heard his voice before, and then I remembered it must have been at the Harpers' dance in March, when he had been rather the worse for drink and said quite shocking things to poor Elsie Martin right in front of everyone. So you can imagine my surprise when I saw him so respectable and proper-looking this afternoon, and him calling Mrs. Westaway "old girl" as if they were old friends! I do wonder how she knows such people, Mamma, and whether Sir William knows what sort of company his wife keeps. Not that it's any business of mine, of course, but one cannot help observing these things when they happen quite in public, can one?

She calls Billy "Duckie,"
and continually pats and caresses him; he does look such a fool, and I
should hate to be fingered like that if I were a man, one must feel
like a bunch of grapes with the bloom being rubbed off. Mrs. Westaway
kept Lord Valmond with her all the rest of the time at the show, and
then took him on the lake while we played croquet.

Lady Bobby went straight to her room and sat by the window, and every
now and then shouted advice to Lord George who was playing with me.
When we had finished, Lady Westaway took me to see the conservatories,
and there we were joined by old Colonel Blake and Lord Valmond, I don't
know how he had torn himself away from Mrs.
pair.prefix:
We had a special reserved tent for tea,
and Mrs. Westaway seemed to have every man in the place round her, and
I heard one man come up and say, "Well, Phyllis, this is a joke to find
you in this respectable hole; how do you like solid matrimony, old
girl?" and I do think that sounded familiar and rude, don't you,
Mamma? but Mrs. Westaway wasn't a bit angry.

source_document.title: The Visits of Elizabeth by Elinor Glyn
